title: Services and Facades Technical Reference
readerIntent: Audit service ownership, context, dependencies, resilience, and tests.
owner: Owning capability and Nodics service contracts
summary: Every service documents its owner, contract, configuration, context, dependencies, side effects, failures, observability, performance, and override path.

sections.heading: Service and facade roles
items: A service owns cohesive business or framework behavior and its invariants. A facade coordinates a use case across owned services without taking their data authority.
Controllers adapt transport, pipelines order processing, models handle provider-neutral persistence, and utilities provide mechanics; none should absorb service decisions.
Name contracts by responsibility, use explicit inputs and outputs, preserve tenant and principal context, and document side effects and idempotency.

sections.heading: Cross-module communication
items: Use DefaultModuleService and configured logical server endpoints for module calls instead of hard-coded URLs or direct imports across runtime boundaries.
Human bearer tokens and internal service tokens remain distinct. The target route verifies audience, tenant, permission, ownership, validation, and business state.
Set timeout, cancellation, retry classification, circuit, response mapping, correlation, and uncertain-outcome handling for every remote dependency.

sections.heading: Customization and transactions
items: Projects override the smallest supported layered service and delegate unchanged behavior instead of copying an entire module.

Transactions stay within provider and authority boundaries. Cross-module processes use idempotency, workflow, compensation, and reconciliation rather than pretending to share one database transaction.
Reusable policy and behavior values belong in properties.js; secrets and endpoints use governed configuration, not constants or package metadata.

sections.heading: Operations and verification
items: Test invariants, denial, boundary values, concurrency, duplicate commands, dependency timeout, cancellation, circuit, partial completion, recovery, and regression.
Measure latency, result category, dependency calls, retries, saturation, and business-safe audit with correlation and bounded labels.
Review ownership, dependency direction, generated model use, cleanup, API compatibility, documentation, and behavior under mono and distributed topology.

sections.heading: Checklist
items: Stable name, owner, input, output, side effects, and idempotency.
Tenant, enterprise, principal, permission, correlation, and transaction context.
Schema, pipeline, event, provider, remote-module, cache, and search dependencies.
Timeout, retry, circuit, cleanup, status codes, logs, metrics, and audit.
Positive, negative, boundary, contract, integration, distributed, security, performance, and regression tests.

sections.heading: Prohibited
items: Business logic in controllers, utilities, generated artifacts, or frontend code.
Direct HTTP clients instead of the governed module service.
Unsafe write retries or human credentials for internal calls.
Hardcoded module URLs, secrets, tenants, or permission decisions.
Detached work without lifecycle, cancellation, durable ownership, correlation, and recovery.

sections.heading: Complete guide: Module Transport Resilience Contract
paragraphs: `DefaultModuleService` is the authoritative HTTP boundary for Nodics module-to-module and governed external calls. Callers continue to use `buildRequest`, `buildExternalRequest`, and `fetch`; projects customize policy through layered `serviceCommunication` properties or a later-loaded same-name service override.

Every request has a bounded deadline and uses shared keep-alive agents. Safe reads may retry transient network failures and configured HTTP statuses with bounded exponential backoff and jitter. Writes retry only when the caller provides an idempotency key. A per-module or per-origin circuit opens after the configured failure threshold and permits a half-open recovery probe after its cooldown.

TLS certificate verification is mandatory. Projects requiring private trust roots must configure the process trust store or override the transport with a verified enterprise CA policy; disabling certificate verification is not a supported resilience option.

Diagnostics expose counts, latency, timeout/retry totals, and circuit state. They never include authorization headers, API keys, request bodies, response bodies, query secrets, or credential material. Runtime shutdown destroys the connection pools through the central lifecycle service.
Provider-specific clients must delegate module HTTP calls to this service rather than adding independent retry, pooling, circuit, or timeout authority paths.
